What AI handles well

AI Is Strongest on Repeatable, Defined Work

AI Strengths

  • Information Support: Surfacing the right knowledge, answer, or documentation at the right moment.
  • Pattern Recognition: Identifying recurring issues and signals across many interactions.
  • Guidance: Providing the next best step based on the situation and known procedures.
  • Workflow Automation: Handling repeatable steps like status checks, reminders, and routine updates.
  • Consistent Process: Applying the same defined steps the same way every time.

Human Strengths

  • Judgment: Weighing context and making the right call when the answer is not obvious.
  • Empathy: Responding to frustration, anxiety, or uncertainty with understanding.
  • Ambiguity: Working through unclear or incomplete situations.
  • Persuasion: Moving a customer toward the right outcome without pressure.
  • Nuanced Troubleshooting: Diagnosing problems that do not fit a standard path.
  • Exceptions: Handling situations that fall outside the defined workflow.

How the work is divided

Four Principles for a Human + AI Operation

Start With the Outcome

Define what the support operation is supposed to achieve before choosing the technology.

Automate the Repeatable

Use AI for defined, repeatable steps where it improves consistency and speed.

Reserve the Human for the Human

Keep human judgment for ambiguity, empathy, and exceptions.

Escalate Clearly

Define when an AI-assisted interaction should move to a person.

Clear answers

Frequently Asked Questions About AI Customer Support

What is AI customer support outsourcing?
AI customer support outsourcing uses AI-enabled tools to support a customer support operation, combining automation for repeatable tasks with human judgment for complex or sensitive conversations.
Does AI replace human support agents?
Not necessarily. AI is best used to handle repeatable work and support human agents, while human judgment remains important for ambiguity, empathy, and exceptions.
What does AI handle well in customer support?
Information support, pattern recognition, guidance, workflow automation, and repeatable processes are areas where AI can improve consistency and speed.
What still requires a human?
Judgment, empathy, ambiguity, persuasion, nuanced troubleshooting, and exceptions are areas where human involvement remains important.
Does SONIQCX charge by the hour for AI support?
No. SONIQCX does not charge clients by the hour. Compensation is tied to the agreed performance outcomes of the engagement.
How does SONIQCX decide what AI should handle?
The decision starts with the customer outcome, then divides work into what can be automated consistently and what requires human judgment, with a clear escalation path between them.
Can AI and human agents work together in the same operation?
Yes. The strongest operations are usually hybrid: AI handles repeatable work and supports humans, while humans handle the conversations that require judgment and empathy.
Does SONIQCX provide AI support nationwide?
Yes. SONIQCX works with businesses nationwide across the United States.

The outcome decides the tool

Automate the Repeatable. Keep the Human Where It Matters.

AI is a tool for producing a better customer outcome, not an end in itself. SONIQCX combines AI-enabled automation with human judgment, and does not charge clients by the hour.

The evaluation framework

Thirteen Questions to Answer Before You Pick a Provider

Define the Customer Problem

Start with what customers actually need help with, not with what a vendor sells.

Define the Support Scope

Establish which issues, channels, and responsibilities are included.

Define Successful Resolution

Agree what "solved" means for each issue category.

Define Escalation

Clarify what moves to another team and what context travels with it.

Define Provider Authority

Establish what the provider can decide and do without asking.

Define Systems and Data

Agree what the provider can access and use to help the customer.

Define Measurement

Establish how the support outcome is tracked and verified.

Define Attribution

Agree how results connect to the operation's work.

Ask How AI Is Used

Understand what is automated and what requires a person.

Ask What Requires a Human

Confirm the provider keeps human judgment for empathy and exceptions.

Compare Commercial Models

Understand whether you are paying for hours, seats, or outcomes.

Ask How Disputes Are Reconciled

Know what happens when a result is questioned.

Ask How Improvement Is Measured

Understand how the provider shows it is getting better over time.

Vendor evaluation checklist

Questions to Put in Front of Any Provider

  • Can the provider define the support scope and issue categories clearly?
  • Does the provider distinguish support quality from raw activity metrics?

What Is Outcome-Based BPO Pricing?

Outcome-based BPO pricing is a commercial model where the outsourcing provider's compensation is tied to agreed measurable results rather than the number of hours, agents, or seats used to perform the work.

Those results depend on the operation.

For a sales program, the outcome might involve completed sales, qualified opportunities, appointments, or another agreed conversion event.

For a retention program, the outcome might involve customers saved, renewed, reactivated, or revenue protected.

For customer service or support, the relevant outcome may involve resolution quality, retention, customer experience, or another clearly defined measure.

SONIQCX does not force every engagement into the same pricing unit.

The pricing structure begins by defining what success means for that specific operation and how it can be measured fairly.

Outcome-based pricing does not ask:“How many hours did the team work?” It asks:“What did the operation produce?”

Pricing inputs that matter

What Determines Outcome-Based BPO Pricing?

There is no responsible universal price for “a result.” A qualified appointment is different from a retained subscriber. A completed sale is different from a support resolution.

The right commercial model depends on the economics, customer journey, measurement quality, and level of control inside the specific program.

The Outcome

The first question is what event or result creates measurable value for the business. The outcome has to be specific enough that both sides know when it occurred.

Value of the Outcome

Different outcomes create different levels of business value. The commercial structure has to make economic sense for both the client and the operation producing the result.

Attribution

The parties need a clear way to determine when SONIQCX activity contributed to the measured outcome. The cleaner the attribution, the cleaner the pricing model can be.

Customer Journey

A short inbound sales conversation behaves differently from a longer retention, support, renewal, or account-growth process. The journey affects how performance is measured.

Available Data

Outcome pricing depends on reliable information. The systems and reporting available to the program affect what can be measured accurately and transparently.

Operational Control

A provider should not pretend to control variables it cannot actually influence. The pricing structure has to reflect which parts of the outcome SONIQCX can reasonably affect.

If the result cannot be verified with agreed data, the model breaks down during reconciliation.

Durability Rules

Define the agreed period a result must remain valid so saves and upgrades reflect lasting value.

Clear Exclusions

A pay-for-performance BPO contract connects provider compensation to measurable business outcomes such as sales, qualified appointments, retention, renewals, resolution, or revenue, rather than billing purely for agent hours or seats.

The contract can include a durability period, a net-result rule, or another agreed mechanism so canceled or refunded transactions are handled fairly.

No. Operational standards can remain in place alongside performance-based outcome requirements.

A disputed outcome can be reviewed using call recordings, CRM data, customer records, scheduling data, and the qualification or attribution rules established in the agreement.

Performance pricing only works when both parties agree on which outcomes were actually influenced or created by the provider.

What Is Performance-Based Customer Retention?

Performance-based customer retention is an outsourced retention model where the operation is built and measured around agreed retention outcomes rather than simply billing the client for agent hours or counting processed cancellations.

Find the churn before the cancellation

Most Retention Problems Begin Before the Cancellation Call.

Customers rarely decide to leave in a single moment. A cancellation request is usually the final step in a longer series of signals that went unnoticed or unresolved.

Reduced Usage

The customer is using the product or service less than before or has stopped engaging with key features.

Unresolved Support

The customer contacted support repeatedly and the underlying problem was never fully resolved.

Payment Problems

Failed payments, declined cards, or billing disputes put the account at risk.

Declining Satisfaction

Survey responses, reviews, or direct feedback show falling confidence in the relationship.

Approaching Expiration

A contract, subscription, or membership period is ending and renewal has not been secured.

Changing Circumstances

The customer's needs changed and no one has explored whether a different plan or arrangement could still fit.

A useful retention operation identifies these signals early and responds before the relationship reaches the point of cancellation.

The right kind of save

Retention Is About Saving Relationships That Should Be Saved. Not Pressuring Every Customer.

A retention operation should not treat every cancellation request as a problem to be blocked at any cost. Some customers genuinely need to leave, and the correct result may be a respectful, compliant cancellation.

Strong retention programs protect the customer experience while trying to preserve the relationship:

  • Discover the real reason for leaving
  • Use approved, relevant save paths
  • Never pressure a customer who should not be pressured
  • Follow clear cancellation and compliance processes
  • Escalate when the customer requires it

The objective is durable retention, not a forced save that unravels later.

Save the relationships that can be saved.Respect the customers who need to leave.

Save durability

A Save That Unravels Next Month Was Never Really a Save.

A customer who agrees to stay during a difficult conversation may still leave shortly after if the underlying problem was not resolved.

Durable retention requires the save to be verified over time, because a save can fail when:

The underlying problem was never resolvedThe customer was offered a discount instead of a solutionThe customer agreed only to end the callThe business changed nothing about the experience

If durability matters, the engagement should define:

Performance-based upselling and cross-selling is an outsourced account-growth model where a provider helps identify and handle legitimate opportunities to expand an existing customer relationship and is measured against agreed outcomes rather than billing the client for agent hours.

Upselling generally means helping a customer move to a higher-value version, tier, capacity level, or expanded version of something they already use.

Cross-selling generally means connecting the customer with an additional related product or service that fits a separate need. The exact definitions vary by business.

SONIQCX does not charge clients by the hour. Compensation is tied to the agreed performance outcomes established for the engagement.

The purpose is not more offers.
The purpose is more relevant customer value.

Upselling vs. Cross-Selling

Two Different Ways to Grow an Existing Customer Relationship

Upselling

The customer moves toward a higher-value version, expanded tier, larger capacity, upgraded package, or another enhanced version of what they already use.

Would a larger or more capable version better fit the customer’s actual need?

Cross-Selling

The customer adds a related product or service that addresses another legitimate need.

Is there another relevant problem the business can help this customer solve?

Both should begin with customer need.
Neither should begin with “what else can we sell?”

Customer Need Before Offer

A Relevant Offer Starts With Context.

The strongest account-growth opportunities are not created by pitching every customer. They come from recognizing when the customer has a need the current product, service, plan, or relationship does not fully address.

01

Context

What is happening in the customer relationship right now?

02

Need

Is there a legitimate additional problem or requirement?

03

Fit

Does an approved additional offer actually address that need?

04

Choice

Can the customer make the decision clearly and without unnecessary pressure?

The exact data and customer context available will vary by engagement.

Protect the Primary Interaction

The Original Customer Need Comes First.

A support interaction is still a support interaction. A billing question is still a billing question. A service problem still needs to be solved. A retention issue still needs to be understood.

If an additional need becomes clear after the customer’s primary reason for contact has been handled appropriately, there may be a legitimate opportunity for another relevant offer.

But the sales opportunity should never take priority over solving the customer’s actual problem.

Solve First. Expand Only When It Fits.

Account-Growth Performance

The Correct Outcome Depends on the Engagement.

01

Upgrade

The customer chooses an agreed higher-value version or expanded option.

02

Additional Purchase

The customer adds another relevant product or service.

03

Account Value

The engagement may measure an agreed increase in customer account value when that measure can be defined responsibly.

04

Incremental Revenue

Revenue may be an appropriate result when the incremental amount can be attributed clearly to the account-growth interaction.

05

Other Agreed Growth Outcome

Some businesses may define account growth differently based on their products, customer lifecycle, and commercial model.

Not every engagement uses every measure. Revenue, account value, or transaction count is not always the commercial unit.

Expansion Quality

A Bigger Transaction Is Not Automatically a Better Customer Outcome.

An account-growth program can create bad incentives if it rewards only immediate transaction value. The customer may buy something that does not fit. The additional purchase may be canceled later. The interaction may reduce trust. The offer may solve the provider’s metric instead of the customer’s need.

That is why the agreed performance outcome should reflect more than offer volume. Depending on the engagement, both sides may choose to define:

  • what counts as a valid growth outcome
  • what does not count
  • whether customer continuation or durability matters
  • how reversals or cancellations are handled
  • what result can reasonably be attributed to SONIQCX
Account growth should create real customer value, not just a larger invoice.
Define the result before performance is measured.

Durability

Does the Customer Need to Keep the Upgrade for the Result to Count? Define It Up Front.

Some businesses may care only that a valid transaction occurred. Others may care whether the upgrade or additional purchase remains active for a defined period. Those are different performance models.

If durability matters, the engagement should define:

  • whether durability is part of the outcome
  • when the result becomes valid
  • how cancellations or reversals are handled
  • how customer-initiated changes are treated
  • which factors remain outside SONIQCX’s control
Durability counts only when the engagement defines it.

Account Growth vs. Retention

Keeping a Customer and Growing a Customer Are Not the Same Objective.

Retention focuses on preserving a customer relationship that is at risk. Upselling and cross-selling focus on creating additional value inside an existing relationship when a legitimate additional need exists.

A retention conversation should not automatically become an expansion conversation. A customer who is considering leaving may first need a problem resolved or confidence restored.

Account Growth vs. Inbound Sales

New Demand and Existing-Customer Growth Require Different Context.

Inbound sales often starts when a customer or prospect initiates a commercial conversation. Account growth starts with an existing customer relationship.

The buyer already has history with the business. That history changes the context of the conversation. The program should understand the existing relationship before presenting an additional offer.

Account-Growth Performance Affects Our Economics Too.

A provider can make more offers while still billing the client for every agent hour. SONIQCX is different.

We do not charge clients by the hour. Our compensation is tied to the agreed performance outcomes established for the upselling and cross-selling engagement.

The exact commercial structure depends on the program. The principle is consistent: we are not paid simply because more sales conversations happened. We are building toward the agreed customer-growth result.

Measurement and Attribution

If Account Growth Determines Performance, the Result Has to Be Clear.

An additional purchase may be influenced by more than one factor. The customer may already have been considering the upgrade. A marketing campaign may have introduced the product. A pricing change may have affected the decision. Another sales team may have played a role.

The engagement should define which customer interactions SONIQCX operates, what qualifies as an opportunity and valid outcome, which agreed data determines the result, how overlapping influence is handled, whether reversals or durability matter, and what SONIQCX can reasonably influence.

04

Credit is limited to growth SONIQCX can reasonably influence.

Protect the Relationship

A Performance Model Should Protect the Customer Relationship.

If the only metric is immediate transaction value, the operation may be encouraged to push offers too aggressively. That is not the model SONIQCX should present.

A responsible account-growth program should protect customer relevance, customer choice, clear communication, appropriate offer fit, and the integrity of the existing relationship.

The exact operating standards are defined by the engagement.

Performance should reward the right result, not the hardest pitch.

Human + AI

Better Account Growth Starts With Better Context.

Upselling and cross-selling require judgment. The operation has to understand the customer’s current situation before deciding whether another offer belongs in the conversation.

AI-enabled tools can support the operation by helping surface information, identify patterns, provide guidance, and automate repeatable workflow tasks where appropriate.

Human judgment remains important when the interaction requires listening, context, empathy, explanation, persuasion, or nuance. The objective is not to automatically pitch the next product. It is to identify when an additional offer genuinely fits.

The program should be built around customer need, offer relevance, clear communication, customer choice, and an agreed definition of a valid outcome rather than the number of offers made.

What is the main difference between traditional BPO and pay-for-performance BPO?
Traditional BPO pricing is usually tied to labor, seats, time, or transaction volume. Pay-for-performance BPO connects provider compensation to measurable business outcomes such as revenue, conversion, retention, or resolution.
Is pay-for-performance BPO cheaper?
Not necessarily. The objective is not simply to pay less. The objective is to connect more of the cost to measurable business value and align the provider's incentives with the client's outcomes.
Does a performance-based BPO still use operational metrics?
Yes. Service levels, response time, staffing, and efficiency still matter. Operational metrics help manage the operation, while performance metrics measure the business outcome.

SONIQCX and the client define the outcome, measurement source, qualification criteria, attribution rules, exclusions, and reporting process before launch.

Potentially. The first step is establishing baseline performance and determining which outcomes the provider can reasonably influence and measure.

No. Operational commitments can remain in place alongside outcome-based performance requirements.

The contract can establish attribution rules and account for client-controlled variables such as pricing, inventory, product changes, fulfillment, or marketing quality.

description: Hourly BPO pricing rewards time and staffing instead of results. See why pay-for-performance outsourcing creates better incentive alignment. SONIQCX does not charge by the hour.
html:
Why Hourly BPO Pricing Fails

The Longer It Takes, the More Your BPO Makes.

That is the fundamental problem with hourly outsourcing: you pay for every agent hour used, so more repeat contacts, inefficient calls, and bloated staffing generate more revenue for the vendor.

SONIQCX believes the financial model should reward better performance instead. Our performance-based approach rewards measurable outcomes: conversion, revenue, retention, resolution, and customer value.

SONIQCX does not charge clients by the hour. Our compensation is tied to the agreed performance outcomes of the engagement.

See a Better Pricing Model Compare the Two Models

Hourly Pricing

Paid for time worked

Performance Pricing

Paid for outcomes produced

Direct answer

What Is Wrong With Hourly Pricing?

Hourly pricing rewards the delivery of labor, not the delivery of results.

When the provider is paid by the hour, efficiency, resolution, and prevention can all work against the provider's revenue. The client is left carrying the performance risk alone.

The issue is not that hourly providers are bad. The issue is that the commercial model is misaligned with the outcome the client actually wants.

Pay for the clock.
Or pay for what happens while it runs.

The provider meets the contract while the business loses

The Invoice Is Paid. The Outcome Is Not.

Conversion Falls

Sales conversion can drop while the total billable agent hours remain fully charged.

Value per Interaction Falls

Agents can treat conversations as throughput tasks instead of opportunities to create value.

Acquisition Cost Rises

The cost of each customer rises as unaligned incentives waste the demand the business already paid to generate.

The Invoice Is Still Due

The provider fulfilled the labor agreement, leaving the client to absorb the performance downside alone.

Structural flaws

Four Structural Flaws of Hourly Pricing.

More Problems Means More Hours

Preventable issues drive repeat contacts, which increases staffing and vendor billing.

Efficiency Reduces Vendor Revenue

If fewer agents can handle the work, the vendor loses billable hours, so there is little incentive to become more efficient.

Headcount Is the Default Answer

Operational surges trigger requests for more seats instead of root-cause fixes.

Focus Narrows to Cost per Hour

The client negotiates hourly rates instead of measuring cost per successful outcome.

Rethinking the economics

Change the Measure and the Behavior Changes.

Handle Time vs. Outcome

Rushing to hit a short-handle-time target can create repeat work. The right measure is the customer outcome, not the clock.

Cost per Resolution

A problem resolved in one interaction is cheaper than the same problem requiring several, even when the per-interaction cost looks lower.

Value-Based Automation

Automation handles repeatable tasks so human judgment is reserved for complex sales, support, and retention conversations.

Shared Upside

When compensation connects to results, the provider has a direct reason to find ways to create more value.

Clear answers about hourly pricing

Frequently Asked Questions About Hourly BPO Pricing

Why is hourly BPO pricing a problem?
Hourly pricing primarily rewards the delivery of labor. The provider is paid based on time worked even when business outcomes such as conversion, retention, or revenue do not improve.
Does hourly pricing always mean poor performance?
No. Many strong providers use hourly pricing. The issue is incentive alignment, not an assumption that hourly providers perform poorly.
Is pay-for-performance always better than hourly pricing?
No. Performance pricing works best when outcomes can be clearly defined, measured, attributed, and meaningfully influenced by the provider.
Why do most BPOs use hourly pricing?
Hourly pricing is simple, predictable, and closely tied to the provider's primary operating cost, which is labor.
Can customer service use performance-based pricing?
Yes. Compensation can be tied to outcomes such as first-contact resolution, repeat-contact reduction, customer satisfaction, and retention when reliable measurement is available.
Can sales outsourcing be paid based on revenue?
Yes. When attribution and the sales process allow it, compensation can be connected to revenue or other agreed outcomes the operation can reasonably influence.
Does SONIQCX still charge operating fees?
SONIQCX does not charge clients by the hour. Compensation is tied to the agreed performance outcomes established for the engagement. The exact commercial structure depends on the program.
How do you measure performance fairly?
The client and SONIQCX define the outcome, source of truth, baseline, attribution rules, exclusions, and verification process before the program begins.
What happens when the client controls part of the result?
Performance terms should account for client-controlled factors such as pricing, inventory, fulfillment, final sales execution, and product quality.
Can an existing hourly BPO be converted to performance pricing?
Potentially. The first step is establishing reliable performance measurement and identifying which outcomes can reasonably be connected to provider activity.

The clock is not the outcome

Stop Paying for the Clock. Start Paying for What Happens While It Is Running.

Hourly BPO pricing tells you how much labor you purchased. It does not tell you how much value that labor created.

SONIQCX builds performance-based outsourcing relationships that connect customer operations to revenue, conversion, retention, resolution, and measurable business outcomes, and we do not charge clients by the hour.
